subtype: Approach: rigid persistence despite weak signals [Pitfall]
passage: Sarita, since you keep saying you'll never quit your delivery idea, let old Dolma tell you mine. In my second year I began a small tea-and-snacks delivery in the hostel. After six months we had maybe ten customers. What did I do? I added things: a mobile app, then a loyalty card, then a fancy menu. My friend and cofounder Pema said, "Dolma, nobody is asking for these things." I said quitting would mean I had failed, and kept going. My attendance fell, my grades fell, and my savings went into features nobody used. Pema left in the eighth month. When I finally stopped, I felt lighter, not smaller. I wish I had listened at month six, when listening was cheap.

qa.q: How many customers did Dolma have after six months?
qa.a: Dolma had maybe ten customers after six months.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Pema said nobody was asking for the new things?
qa.a: Dolma felt defensive and afraid of failing, treating quitting as proof of failure, so Dolma kept going.

qa.q: What choice at month six could Dolma have made instead, and why?
qa.a: Dolma could have asked customers why so few ordered, then changed the plan around the answers, because more features answered a question nobody had asked.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt watching Dolma add more and more features?
qa.a: Pema likely felt worried and unheard, having spoken plainly at month six and then leaving in the eighth month.

grounding: Shows rigid persistence: months of few customers, more features, no change of direction, and rising costs to grades and savings.

subtype: Approach: rigid persistence despite weak signals [Pitfall]
passage: Six months into his campus bike-rental app, Tenzin had eleven regular users out of three thousand students. His cofounder Anand showed him the numbers in the hostel mess. "Maybe we should change something. Or pause." Tenzin shook his head. "Quitting is what failures do." Instead he added features: a leaderboard, bike reviews, a referral bonus. Each took weeks of coding at night. His mid-semester marks dropped in two subjects, and his savings from summer work thinned with every server bill. Then came the complication: the college announced its own free cycle scheme for the new semester. Anand pleaded, "Can we at least talk to the eleven users and ask why they stay?" Tenzin stared at the announcement on his phone. "We just need one more feature." That night he started coding a chat function, with an exam the next morning.

qa.q: How many regular users did Tenzin have?
qa.a: Eleven regular users out of three thousand students.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin refuse to change the plan?
qa.a: Tenzin feels that quitting would make him a failure, and that fear keeps him stubbornly adding features.

qa.q: What would you change first in Tenzin's approach?
qa.a: Talk to the eleven users as Anand suggests, and set a clear point to change direction or pause, especially with exams and savings at stake.

qa.q: How is Anand affected by Tenzin's persistence?
qa.a: Anand grows worried and frustrated, pleading to talk to users while Tenzin keeps coding features nobody asked for.

grounding: Shows a founder with few customers after six months adding features and refusing to change course, believing quitting means failure, while grades and savings suffer.

subtype: Approach: rigid persistence despite weak signals [Pitfall]
passage: In their rented room in Pune, Zubin's whiteboard still said "Target: 1,000 users by March." It was now September of the following year. The notes-sharing site he had built with Harish had forty-two users, most of them friends. Harish had stopped coming to the weekly meeting. "The signs are clear, Zubin. People share notes in their class groups for free." Zubin rubbed out the old target and wrote "Version 3: dark mode, badges, auto summaries." "Once they see the new features, they'll come." His semester results arrived that week: two backlogs. His internship savings were almost gone, spent on hosting and ads. His mother called. "Beta, you sound tired." "I'm fine, Ma. I just can't give up now. Giving up means it was all a waste." He hung up and went back to designing badges.

qa.q: How many users did the site have?
qa.a: Forty-two users, most of them friends.

qa.q: Why does Zubin keep going despite the signs?
qa.a: Zubin dreads that giving up would mean it was all a waste, and that fear keeps him adding features.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do instead of Version 3?
qa.a: Zubin could ask the forty-two users what they value, set a clear test with a deadline, and pause if it fails, protecting grades and savings.

qa.q: How is Harish affected by Zubin's refusal?
qa.a: Harish has lost faith and stopped attending meetings, having seen that people share notes for free.

grounding: Illustrates a founder who keeps adding features to a product few people use, refusing to change plan because quitting feels like failure, as grades and savings suffer.
